chapter.title: Waves
chapter.description: Study the propagation of disturbances, mechanical waves, transverse and longitudinal waves, progressive waves, wave speed, superposition, reflection, standing waves, normal modes and beats.

topics.title: What is a Wave?
topics.content: A wave is a disturbance that travels from one place to another. The wave moves, but the matter it travels through does not move along with it.

topics.title: Energy Transfer
topics.content: A wave carries energy and information from one point to another — it does not carry matter with it.

topics.title: Mechanical Waves
topics.content: Mechanical waves need a material medium (like a string, water, or air) to travel through. Waves on a string, water waves, sound waves and earthquake waves are all mechanical waves.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Waves
topics.content: Electromagnetic waves do not need a medium — they can travel even through empty space (vacuum). Light, radio waves and X-rays are examples.

topics.title: Matter Waves
topics.content: Matter waves are linked to tiny particles like electrons, protons, neutrons, atoms and molecules.

topics.title: Wave Propagation in a Medium
topics.content: A disturbance moves through a medium because the particles are connected — when one particle moves, it pulls or pushes its neighbour, and so the disturbance passes along the whole chain.

topics.title: Transverse Waves
topics.definition: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium move up and down (or side to side), at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
examples: Wave on a stretched string
topics.importantPoint: Particle motion is perpendicular to the wave's direction of travel.

topics.title: Longitudinal Waves
topics.definition: In a longitudinal wave, the particles of the medium move back and forth along the same direction the wave travels.
examples: Sound waves in air
topics.importantPoint: Particle motion is parallel to the wave's direction of travel — look for compressions and rarefactions, not crests and troughs.

topics.title: Compressions and Rarefactions
topics.content: As a longitudinal sound wave travels, it creates regions where particles are squeezed close together (compressions) and regions where they spread apart (rarefactions).

topics.title: Progressive Waves
topics.definition: A progressive (or travelling) wave moves steadily from one part of the medium to another, even though the medium as a whole stays in place.

topics.title: Propagation in Different Media
topics.content: Transverse waves need a medium that can resist being twisted or sheared, so they mainly travel through solids. Longitudinal waves only need to be compressed, so they can travel through solids, liquids and gases.

topics.title: Water Waves
topics.content: Water waves are a mix of both types — the water particles move in loops, partly up-and-down and partly back-and-forth.

sections.title: Displacement Relation in a Progressive Wave

topics.title: Wave Function
topics.description: This formula describes a smooth, repeating (sinusoidal) wave moving in the positive x-direction.

topics.title: Wave Travelling in Negative Direction
topics.content: This is the same kind of wave, just travelling in the opposite (negative x) direction.

topics.title: Amplitude
topics.definition: Amplitude is how far the particles of the medium move from their resting (equilibrium) position at most.
examples: Doubling the amplitude of a wave increases the energy it carries four-fold, since energy is proportional to a².
On a y(x,t) = a sin(kx − ωt) graph, a is the height of the curve above the axis.
topics.importantPoint: Amplitude is always taken as positive — it's the maximum displacement from equilibrium, in either direction.

topics.title: Phase
topics.definition: The phase tells you exactly where a particle is in its up-and-down cycle at a given place and time.
examples: Two particles exactly one wavelength apart always share the same phase — they move in perfect step.
topics.importantPoint: Phase (kx − ωt + φ) tells you exactly where a particle is in its oscillation cycle, at a given position and time.

topics.title: Initial Phase
topics.definition: The initial phase is the phase value at the starting point, x = 0 and t = 0.
topics.importantPoint: φ shifts the wave sideways along x (or in time) without changing its shape, amplitude, or wavelength.

topics.title: Wavelength
topics.definition: Wavelength is the shortest distance between two points on a wave that are in the exact same stage of their motion (for example, crest to crest).
examples: The distance from one crest to the next crest, or from one compression to the next compression.
λ = 2π/k links the spatial period directly to the angular wave number.
topics.importantPoint: Wavelength is a spatial period, measured in metres — the distance over which the wave pattern repeats.

topics.title: Angular Wave Number
examples: A wave with wavelength 2 m has angular wave number k = 2π/2 = π rad/m.
topics.importantPoint: k = 2π/λ is the spatial analogue of ω — radians per metre instead of radians per second.
topics.content: It tells you how many radians of the wave shape fit into one metre.

topics.title: Time Period
examples: The time taken for any one particle in the medium to complete one full oscillation.
Halving the angular frequency ω doubles the time period, since T = 2π/ω.
topics.importantPoint: Time period is a temporal period — the wave's spatial twin is the wavelength.
topics.content: It is measured in seconds.

topics.title: Angular Frequency
examples: A wave completing 5 oscillations per second (ν = 5 Hz) has ω = 2π(5) ≈ 31.4 rad/s.
topics.importantPoint: ω = 2πν — angular frequency is frequency measured in radians per second instead of cycles per second.
topics.content: It tells you how fast the wave oscillates, in radians per second.

topics.title: Frequency
examples: A tuning fork vibrating at 440 Hz completes 440 oscillations every second.
A shorter time period always means a higher frequency, since ν = 1/T.
topics.importantPoint: Frequency and time period are reciprocals of each other: ν = 1/T.
topics.content: It is measured in hertz (Hz) — one hertz means one oscillation per second.

topics.content: This gives the displacement of a particle in a longitudinal wave, at any position and time.

sections.title: The Speed of a Travelling Wave

topics.title: Wave Speed
examples: Sound travels through air at roughly 343 m/s at room temperature.
v = ω/k gives the speed at which a fixed phase point, such as a crest, moves.
topics.importantPoint: Wave speed is fixed by the medium's properties — it does not depend on the wave's amplitude or frequency.
topics.content: It is how fast the wave pattern moves through the medium, in metres per second.

topics.title: Fundamental Wave Relation
examples: If λ = 0.5 m and ν = 660 Hz, then v = λν = 330 m/s, close to the speed of sound in air.
topics.importantPoint: v = λν connects every core wave property in one line: speed, wavelength, and frequency.
topics.content: This links a wave's speed, wavelength and frequency in one simple equation.

topics.title: Physical Meaning
topics.content: In the time it takes a particle to complete one full oscillation, the wave itself moves forward by exactly one wavelength.

topics.title: Dependence of Wave Speed
topics.content: How fast a mechanical wave travels depends only on the medium's mass (inertia) and stiffness (elasticity) — not on the wave's amplitude or frequency.

sections.title: The Principle of Superposition of Waves

topics.title: Superposition Principle
topics.definition: When two or more waves meet at a point, the total displacement there is just the sum of what each wave would cause on its own.
examples: Two ripples crossing on a pond simply pass through each other, each carrying on unaffected afterward.
topics.importantPoint: Waves don't collide like particles — their displacements simply add together, point by point, and each wave continues on its own way.

topics.title: Multiple Waves
topics.content: When several waves overlap at once, you just add up all their individual displacements.

topics.title: Interference
topics.content: Interference is what happens when two or more waves overlap and add together — it follows directly from the superposition principle.

topics.title: Constructive Interference
examples: Two loudspeakers in phase produce a louder sound where their waves overlap and reinforce.
topics.importantPoint: Constructive interference occurs when the path or phase difference is a whole number of wavelengths (0, λ, 2λ, …).
topics.content: The two waves line up crest-to-crest, so they add up to make a bigger wave.

topics.title: Destructive Interference
examples: Noise-cancelling headphones generate a wave out of phase with unwanted sound so the two cancel.
topics.importantPoint: Destructive interference occurs when the path or phase difference is an odd multiple of half a wavelength (λ/2, 3λ/2, …).
topics.content: The two waves line up crest-to-trough, so they cancel each other out.

topics.title: Resultant Amplitude
topics.importantPoint: A(φ) = 2a cos(φ/2) is maximum (2a) when φ = 0, and zero when φ = π.
topics.content: This gives the amplitude of the combined wave for any phase difference between the two waves.

topics.title: Reflection at a Rigid Boundary
topics.content: When a wave hits a fixed, rigid boundary (like a wall), it bounces back flipped upside down.
examples: A pulse sent down a string tied to a wall comes back upside-down.
topics.importantPoint: A rigid boundary forces zero displacement there, so the reflected wave is always phase-inverted (a 180° flip).

topics.title: Reflection at an Open Boundary
topics.content: When a wave hits a free, open boundary, it bounces back the same way up, without flipping.
examples: A pulse on a string with a free end comes back the same way up, with no inversion.
topics.importantPoint: A free boundary allows maximum displacement there, so the reflected wave keeps the same phase — no inversion.

topics.title: Rigid Boundary
topics.content: This gives the displacement of the reflected wave after it bounces off a rigid (fixed) boundary.

topics.title: Open Boundary
topics.content: This gives the displacement of the reflected wave after it bounces off a free (open) boundary.

topics.title: Echo
topics.content: An echo is simply a sound wave reflecting off a hard, rigid surface and coming back to your ear.
topics.importantPoint: The human ear needs about 0.1 s between a sound and its reflection to hear them as separate — this sets the minimum distance for an audible echo.

topics.title: Standing Wave Formation
topics.description: A standing wave is formed when two identical waves travel in opposite directions and overlap — the wave pattern appears to stay in place instead of moving forward.
examples: A guitar string plucked between two fixed ends sets up a standing wave with fixed nodes at both ends.
topics.importantPoint: A standing wave forms when two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose — no net energy travels along the medium.

topics.title: Nodes
topics.definition: Nodes are points on a standing wave that never move — the displacement there is always zero.
examples: On a string fixed at both ends, the two fixed ends are always nodes.
topics.importantPoint: Nodes are points of zero displacement — they never move, however large the wave's amplitude gets.

topics.title: Antinodes
topics.definition: Antinodes are points on a standing wave that move the most — the displacement there is always at its maximum.
topics.importantPoint: Antinodes are points of maximum displacement, located exactly midway between two consecutive nodes.

topics.title: Distance Between Successive Nodes
topics.content: Two neighbouring nodes on a standing wave are always half a wavelength apart.

topics.title: Distance Between Successive Antinodes
topics.content: Two neighbouring antinodes on a standing wave are always half a wavelength apart.

topics.title: String Fixed at Both Ends
examples: A string of length 0.6 m fixed at both ends can only vibrate at frequencies νₙ = nv/2L, for whole numbers n.
topics.importantPoint: Only wavelengths that fit a whole number of half-wavelengths into the string's length are allowed: L = nλ/2.
topics.content: Only certain wavelengths fit neatly onto a string fixed at both ends — this formula shows which ones are allowed.

topics.title: Harmonics
topics.content: The lowest frequency a string can vibrate at is called the fundamental (or first harmonic). The next allowed frequencies are the second harmonic, third harmonic, and so on.
topics.importantPoint: The lowest possible frequency is the fundamental (1st harmonic); every allowed frequency above it is a higher harmonic.

topics.title: Air Column Closed at One End
topics.content: In a pipe that is closed at one end, the closed end must be a node, so only the odd-numbered harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th…) can form.
topics.importantPoint: The closed end is always a displacement node, so only odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, …) can form.

topics.title: Open Pipe
topics.content: In a pipe that is open at both ends, both ends are antinodes, so every harmonic — odd and even — can form.
topics.importantPoint: Both ends are displacement antinodes, so an open pipe supports every harmonic — odd and even.

topics.title: Resonance
topics.content: Resonance happens when something is pushed at a frequency very close to its own natural frequency, causing it to vibrate with a much larger amplitude.
examples: Pushing a swing at exactly its natural frequency builds a large amplitude with very little effort.
topics.importantPoint: Resonance occurs when a driving frequency matches a system's natural frequency, producing a sharp rise in amplitude.

example.title: Resonance in an Open Pipe
example.result: The source resonates with the second harmonic of the open pipe.

topics.title: Formation of Beats
topics.definition: Beats happen when two sound waves of slightly different frequency, but similar loudness, overlap.
topics.importantPoint: Beats arise from superposing two waves of slightly different frequency — the resultant amplitude itself rises and falls periodically.

topics.title: Beat Frequency
examples: A tuning fork at 256 Hz and one at 260 Hz sounded together produce 4 beats per second.
topics.importantPoint: Beat frequency is simply the difference of the two frequencies: νbeat = |ν1 − ν2| — musicians use this to tune instruments by listening for the beats to slow and vanish.
topics.content: It is measured in hertz (Hz) — the number of beats you hear each second.

topics.title: Nature of Beats
topics.content: During beats, the loudness of the sound keeps rising and falling in a regular pattern, so you hear it get louder and softer over and over.
topics.importantPoint: The beat pattern repeats with a period of 1/|ν1 − ν2| — frequencies close together produce slow beats you can count by ear.

summary: Mechanical waves exist in material media.
Transverse waves have particle oscillations perpendicular to propagation.
Longitudinal waves have particle oscillations parallel to propagation.
A progressive wave moves from one point of a medium to another.
A sinusoidal wave travelling in the positive x-direction is represented by y(x,t) = a sin(kx - ωt + φ).
Wavelength is the distance between consecutive points having the same phase.
Wave speed v = ω/k = λ/T = λν.
Speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string is v = √(T/μ).
Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves and can propagate through solids, liquids and gases.
The speed of a longitudinal wave is v = √(B/ρ).
The principle of superposition states that resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of individual displacements.
Reflection at a rigid boundary produces a phase change of π.
Standing waves contain nodes and antinodes.
A string fixed at both ends has frequencies νn = nv/(2L).
An air column closed at one end supports odd harmonics.
Beats occur when two waves of slightly different frequencies are superposed.
pointsToPonder: A wave is not motion of matter as a whole in a medium.
Energy, rather than matter, is transferred from one point to another.
Mechanical wave energy transfer occurs through elastic coupling between neighbouring oscillating parts.
Transverse waves require a medium with shear elasticity.
Longitudinal waves can propagate in solids, liquids and gases.
In a harmonic progressive wave, particles have the same amplitude but different phases.
In a stationary wave, particles between two nodes have the same phase but different amplitudes.
The speed of a mechanical wave in a medium depends on the elastic and inertial properties of the medium.
